structure.title: A quarrel within the army
structure.text: Achilles' conflict with Agamemnon changes the balance of the war and the obligations between comrades.

structure.title: Battle and human cost
structure.text: The poem alternates combat, councils, divine interventions, and domestic encounters. It covers a short period, not the whole Trojan War.

people.name: Achilles
people.text: The greatest warrior among the Greeks besieging Troy, who quarrels with his commander over a captive woman and withdraws from the fighting.

people.name: Agamemnon
people.text: The leader of the Greek army, powerful and proud, whose insult to Achilles sets the poem's anger in motion.

people.name: Hector
people.text: Troy's greatest defender, a son of King Priam, who fights for his city knowing what defeat would mean for his wife and son.

context.title: Honour and prizes
context.text: Public recognition distributes status among warriors. Taking a prize can deny the value of the service that earned it.
context.takeaway: The quarrel concerns standing as well as possession.

context.title: Gods in the action
context.text: Gods pursue attachments and rivalries through human events. Divine involvement does not make human pain or choice disappear.
context.takeaway: Read both levels of agency together.

notice.why: Even a short encounter can disclose a life beyond the battlefield.

notice.text: Follow similes from farming and domestic work.
notice.why: Ordinary life remains present inside extraordinary violence.

opening: Achilles refuses to fight because his commander has humiliated him. He is the army's best warrior, and he wants the Greeks to discover how badly they need him, even if that means watching them die. Across the battlefield, Hector returns briefly to his wife and child before going out again. Homer gives both armies people worth mourning. The glory is real, but so are the bodies, and a man's wounded pride can become a disaster that thousands of families have to live through.
